questions.title: What is a Solution Architect responsible for on a MERN project?
questions.quick: I own the shape of the whole solution so that it meets the business need within real constraints. That means turning goals into quality targets, choosing the main building blocks across React, Node, MongoDB and the cloud, recording key decisions, and checking that delivery follows them. I also manage risk, cost and integration with other systems, and I explain trade-offs to clients and developers alike. I stay close to the team, but I do not write every feature.
questions.revision: A Solution Architect owns end-to-end fit: requirements to quality targets, key decisions, integration, risk and cost, then guides and verifies delivery.
questions.detailed:
A Solution Architect is accountable for a **solution that works as a whole**: business goals, user journeys, technology, operations and cost, not one component.

## Core responsibilities

| Area | What it looks like on a MERN project |
|---|---|
| Requirements to design | Turn goals into functional scope and measurable quality targets (latency, availability, security) |
| Structure | Choose the main building blocks: React front end, Node API layer, MongoDB, queues, identity, hosting |
| Decisions | Record important choices and their reasons in short decision records |
| Integration | Define contracts with payment, CRM, identity and legacy systems |
| Risk and cost | Keep a visible list of technical risks, assumptions and a running cost estimate |
| Delivery guidance | Review designs, unblock the team, check that the build matches the intent |
| Communication | Explain the same design to executives, product owners and developers at the right depth |

{{diagram:sa-scope}}

## What it is not

- Not a person who hands down diagrams and disappears. Designs only count when they are built and operated.
- Not the person who must approve every pull request.
- Not a technology evangelist. The goal is fit for the problem, not the newest tool.

## How to answer in an interview

Name a small number of outputs you would produce: a context diagram, a short list of quality targets, a decision log and a risk register. Then say how you check delivery, for example through design reviews and automated checks.

## Common mistakes

- Describing the role only as "choosing technologies".
- Ignoring operations, cost and security until late.
- Designing in isolation from the developers who must build it.
- Producing heavy documents nobody reads instead of short, living ones.

Example (hypothetical): for a customer portal, the architect agrees availability and response targets with the client, selects a modular Node API with MongoDB, defines the identity integration, and reviews the first slice end to end.
followUps: Which outputs would you produce in the first two weeks?
How do you stay credible with developers if you write less code?
Where does your responsibility end and the engineering lead's begin?

diagrams.title: Solution Architect scope
diagrams.alt: The Solution Architect connects business goals to quality targets, key decisions and integration design, then guides delivery and reviews the result while managing risk and cost throughout.

questions.title: Solution Architect versus Software Architect, Technical Architect and Engineering Lead: what is the difference?
questions.quick: The titles overlap and vary by company, so I explain the typical focus. A solution architect looks across the whole solution and its business fit. A software architect goes deep on the structure of one application. A technical architect often owns technology standards and platform choices. An engineering lead manages the team's delivery, people and day-to-day quality. In small teams one person may do several of these.
questions.revision: Solution: whole-solution fit. Software: internal structure of an application. Technical: platform and standards. Engineering lead: team delivery and people. Titles overlap.
questions.detailed:
These titles are **not standardised**. Always clarify how the organisation uses them, then describe the usual centre of gravity of each.

## Typical focus

| Role | Main question | Typical scope | Typical outputs |
|---|---|---|---|
| Solution Architect | Does the whole solution meet the business need within constraints? | Several systems, vendors, teams | Context view, quality targets, integration design, cost and risk |
| Software Architect | How should this application be structured? | One application or product | Module boundaries, patterns, code-level guidelines |
| Technical Architect | Which technology, platform and standards do we use? | Platform, tooling, cloud | Reference architectures, standards, technology choices |
| Engineering Lead | Is the team delivering well and growing? | One team | Planning, code review, mentoring, delivery health |

{{diagram:sa-roles}}

## How they work together

The solution architect frames the problem and the boundaries. The software architect shapes the internals of each part. The technical architect keeps the platform consistent across projects. The engineering lead turns the plan into steady delivery and looks after people.

## In a MERN context

A solution architect may decide that a portal needs a React front end, a Node API, MongoDB and a payment integration. The software architect defines how the Node code is layered. The technical architect keeps the logging, deployment and security baseline common. The lead runs the sprint.

## Common mistakes

- Claiming strict boundaries that do not exist in most companies.
- Treating the architect as above the team rather than part of it.
- Forgetting that in small teams one person covers several roles, so the skill set matters more than the title.

Example (hypothetical): on a small project one senior engineer acts as solution architect and lead; the answer is to name which hat you are wearing in each decision.
followUps: Which role would you combine in a team of six?
How do you avoid overlap and confusion between these roles?
How does the answer change in a consulting company versus a product company?

diagrams.title: Architect role focus
diagrams.alt: Four roles with different focus: the Solution Architect covers the whole solution, the Software Architect covers application structure, the Technical Architect covers platform and standards, and the Engineering Lead covers team delivery.

questions.title: How do you set architecture principles and handle constraints?
questions.quick: Principles are a few short, testable rules that guide many decisions, such as prefer managed services, or APIs are the only way to share data. Constraints are fixed limits like budget, deadline, existing systems, regulations and team skills. I write both down at the start, agree them with the client, and check designs against them. When a principle must be broken, I record the reason in a decision record.
questions.revision: Principles guide choices; constraints limit them. Keep few, testable, agreed with stakeholders, and record any justified exception.
questions.detailed:
**Principles** are chosen guidance; **constraints** are imposed limits. Mixing them up leads to arguments about things nobody can change.

## Constraints versus principles

| | Constraint | Principle |
|---|---|---|
| Origin | Given: budget, date, regulation, existing contracts, team skills | Chosen by the team and sponsor |
| Negotiable? | Rarely | Yes, with a recorded reason |
| Example | Data must stay in one region | Prefer managed services over self-hosting |

## What makes a good principle

1. **Short and memorable**, one sentence.
2. **Includes a reason**, so people can apply it to new cases.
3. **Testable**: a reviewer can say whether a design follows it.
4. **Has a trade-off**: if nobody could choose the opposite, it is not a principle.

```text
Principle: Services share data only through APIs or events.
Reason: lets teams change storage without coordinated releases.
Implication: no direct reads of another service's collections.
```

## Process

1. List constraints with the client at kickoff and mark which are fixed.
2. Propose five to ten principles, discuss, and agree them.
3. Use them in design reviews as a checklist.
4. Where possible, turn them into automated checks (lint rules, dependency checks, pipeline gates).
5. When an exception is needed, write a short decision record and set a review date.

## Common mistakes

- Dozens of vague principles such as "be scalable".
- Treating assumptions as constraints without checking them.
- Writing principles once and never using them in reviews.
- Allowing silent exceptions that erode trust in the rules.

Example (hypothetical): a client has a fixed launch date and a small team. The principle "buy before build" and the constraint "launch in one quarter" together favour a managed identity service over a custom one.
followUps: How would you turn a principle into an automated check?
What do you do when a constraint turns out to be an assumption?
How many principles are too many?

questions.title: How do you run a trade-off analysis using ATAM-lite and a weighted decision matrix?
questions.quick: I gather the key stakeholders, agree the top few quality attributes, and write a scenario for each. Then I walk each candidate option through those scenarios, noting risks, sensitivity points and trade-offs. For the final comparison I use a weighted decision matrix, but I treat the numbers as a conversation aid, not proof. Weights come from the stakeholders, and I test whether the ranking changes when weights shift.
questions.revision: ATAM-lite: agree top quality scenarios, walk options through them, note risks and trade-offs. Weighted matrix summarises; test sensitivity of weights.
questions.detailed:
ATAM (Architecture Tradeoff Analysis Method) is a structured way to evaluate an architecture against quality goals. A **lite** version fits a small team in a half-day workshop.

## ATAM-lite steps

1. **Present the business goals** and constraints in a few minutes.
2. **Pick three to five quality attributes** that matter most (for example availability, change speed, cost).
3. **Write a scenario for each** with a measurable response.
4. **Describe the candidate options** briefly.
5. **Walk each option through each scenario.** Record:
   - **Risks**: decisions that may cause trouble.
   - **Sensitivity points**: parameters where small changes matter a lot.
   - **Trade-offs**: where improving one attribute hurts another.
6. **Summarise** and agree actions.

## Weighted decision matrix

| Criterion | Weight | Option A: modular monolith | Option B: microservices |
|---|---|---|---|
| Time to first release | 5 | 4 | 2 |
| Independent scaling | 3 | 2 | 5 |
| Operational simplicity | 4 | 5 | 2 |
| **Weighted total** (sum of weight x score) | | 20+6+20 = 46 | 10+15+8 = 33 |

Compute the total as the sum of weight times score. The scores above are illustrative.

{{diagram:sa-tradeoff}}

## Using the matrix honestly

- Let **stakeholders set weights**, not the architect alone.
- Run a **sensitivity check**: change a weight and see whether the winner flips. If it does, the decision depends on a value judgement worth discussing.
- Add a **not scored** note for risks that numbers hide, such as team skill gaps.

## Common mistakes

- Scoring first and discussing later, so the matrix justifies a pre-made choice.
- Too many criteria that dilute the important ones.
- Treating a small score difference as decisive.
- Skipping scenarios, so scores are opinions without evidence.

Example (hypothetical): two options score within a few points; the workshop shows the real difference is team familiarity, which becomes a recorded risk with mitigation.
followUps: How would you handle stakeholders who disagree on the weights?
How do scenarios make the scores less subjective?
When is a full ATAM worth the cost?

diagrams.title: Trade-off analysis flow
diagrams.alt: Business goals lead to prioritised quality scenarios; each candidate option is walked through the scenarios to find risks and trade-offs, summarised in a weighted matrix, checked for sensitivity and then recorded as a decision.

questions.title: What is the C4 model and when do you use each level?
questions.quick: C4 describes software at four zoom levels. Context shows my system, its users and neighbouring systems. Containers show the deployable parts such as the React app, Node API and MongoDB. Components show the major building blocks inside one container. Code is optional detail, usually generated. I start with context and containers for clients and new joiners, and drop to components only where the design is complex or risky.
questions.revision: C4: Context (system and neighbours), Container (deployable parts), Component (inside a container), Code (optional). Start high; zoom only where needed.
questions.detailed:
The **C4 model** gives a shared vocabulary for architecture diagrams by zooming in four levels, like a map.

## The four levels

| Level | Shows | Audience | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. System Context | Your system, users, external systems | Everyone, including non-technical | Scope and integration agreement |
| 2. Container | Separately runnable parts: React app, Node API, MongoDB, queue, identity provider | Developers, ops, architects | Technology choices and communication paths |
| 3. Component | Major building blocks inside one container | Developers on that part | Explaining a complex service |
| 4. Code | Classes or modules | Developers | Rarely drawn by hand; generate if needed |

{{diagram:sa-c4}}

Note that a **container** here means any separately runnable unit, not necessarily a Docker container.

## Rules that keep diagrams useful

- Every box has a **name, type and short description** (for example "Orders API, Node.js, handles checkout").
- Every arrow has a **label** saying what flows and how (for example "HTTPS/JSON").
- Include a **legend** and a title stating the level.
- One diagram, one purpose; split instead of cramming.

## Supporting diagrams

C4 covers static structure. Add other views when the question needs them: sequence diagrams for ordering of calls, deployment diagrams for environments and networks, and data-flow diagrams for where sensitive data travels.

## Common mistakes

- Mixing levels, such as a class inside a context diagram.
- Unlabelled arrows and generic boxes labelled "Service".
- Drawing level 4 by hand and letting it go stale.
- Producing diagrams once and never updating them; keep them as text (for example in version control) so they change with the code.

Example (hypothetical): a booking portal's context diagram shows customers, staff and a payment provider; the container diagram shows the React app, Node API, MongoDB and a job worker.
followUps: Which level would you show a client sponsor and why?
How do you keep C4 diagrams from going stale?
When would a sequence diagram be better than a component diagram?

diagrams.title: C4 zoom levels
diagrams.alt: The C4 model zooms from system context to containers, then to components inside a container, and optionally to code, each level adding detail for a more technical audience.

questions.title: What is API-first or contract-first development, and why use it?
questions.quick: API-first means I design the interface before writing the implementation. I describe it in an OpenAPI document, review it with front-end developers, consumers and security, and agree it as the contract. Then the React team can build against a mock while the Node team implements the real thing, and tests check that the service matches the contract. It reduces rework and surprises at integration time.
questions.revision: Design the API contract first (OpenAPI), review with consumers, mock it, build both sides in parallel, and test that the implementation matches.
questions.detailed:
**API-first** treats the API as a product with its own design step. **Contract-first** means the written contract (for example OpenAPI) is the source of truth that both sides follow.

## Workflow

1. **Collect use cases** from consumers: the React app, partners, mobile clients.
2. **Draft the contract** in OpenAPI: resources, operations, schemas, error format, authentication, pagination.
3. **Review** with front-end, back-end, security and QA.
4. **Generate a mock** from the contract so the front end can start immediately.
5. **Implement** the service; validate requests and responses against the contract.
6. **Test the contract** in the pipeline and flag breaking changes.

```yaml
paths:
  /orders/{id}:
    get:
      summary: Get an order
      responses:
        "200": { description: The order }
        "404": { description: Not found }
```

{{diagram:sa-apifirst}}

## Benefits and costs

| Benefit | Cost or risk |
|---|---|
| Parallel front-end and back-end work | Upfront design time |
| Fewer integration surprises | Contract can drift if not enforced |
| Consistent errors, naming, security | Needs discipline on versioning |
| Generated docs, clients and tests | Tooling to set up |

## Keeping it honest

- **Lint** the contract for naming and error rules.
- Run **breaking-change detection** on every pull request.
- Prefer **additive changes**; version only when you must break.
- Use **consumer-driven contract tests** when several teams depend on you.

## Common mistakes

- Writing the spec after the code, so it describes accidents.
- Generating the spec from code and never reviewing it as a design.
- Designing endpoints around database tables instead of consumer needs.
- No error model, so every endpoint fails differently.

Example (hypothetical): a checkout API is agreed in a review, mocked for the React team in the first days, and then validated by tests as the Node service is built.
followUps: How do you detect breaking changes automatically?
When would you choose code-first instead?
How do consumer-driven contract tests fit in?

diagrams.title: API-first workflow
diagrams.alt: Consumer use cases lead to an OpenAPI contract that is reviewed; a mock lets the front end start while the back end is implemented, and contract tests in the pipeline check that the implementation matches.

questions.title: What is the Twelve-Factor App and how does it apply to Node services?
questions.quick: The Twelve-Factor App is a set of habits for building services that run well in the cloud. For a Node service, the big ones are: one codebase with many deploys, explicit dependencies in package files, configuration from the environment, backing services as attached resources, stateless processes, logs as an event stream, and fast start and graceful shutdown. Following them makes deployment, scaling and recovery much more predictable.
questions.revision: Twelve factors make services portable and scalable: config in environment, stateless processes, attached backing services, logs to stdout, disposable processes, dev-prod parity.
questions.detailed:
The **Twelve-Factor App** is a methodology for building software-as-a-service apps that are portable, scalable and easy to deploy.

## The factors applied to Node and MERN

| Factor | Practical meaning for a Node service |
|---|---|
| Codebase | One repository per deployable, many deploys (dev, test, prod) from it |
| Dependencies | Declared in package.json with a lockfile; no hidden global tools |
| Config | Read from environment variables, never committed |
| Backing services | MongoDB, queues and caches are replaceable URLs from config |
| Build, release, run | Separate stages; the same artefact moves between environments |
| Processes | Stateless; sessions and files live in external stores |
| Port binding | Service listens on a port from config |
| Concurrency | Scale by running more processes or containers |
| Disposability | Fast start; handle SIGTERM and finish in-flight requests |
| Dev-prod parity | Use the same kinds of services locally, for example via containers |
| Logs | Write structured events to stdout; the platform collects them |
| Admin processes | Migrations and scripts run as one-off commands in the same release |

```js
const port = Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000);
const mongoUrl = process.env.MONGO_URL; // required
if (!mongoUrl) throw new Error("MONGO_URL is required");

const server = app.listen(port);
process.on("SIGTERM", () => server.close(() => process.exit(0)));
```

## Where it needs adjusting

- **Secrets** deserve a secrets manager, not just plain environment variables.
- **Long-running jobs** and **WebSocket state** need explicit design for statelessness.
- Some teams add factors such as observability and API-first.

## Common mistakes

- Saving uploads or sessions on local disk.
- Different config files committed per environment.
- Logging to files inside the container.
- Ignoring shutdown signals, causing dropped requests during deploys.

Example (hypothetical): a service reads its database URL from the environment, so the same container image runs in test and production with different values.
followUps: Which factor do teams most often break, and how do you detect it?
How do you handle secrets beyond environment variables?
How does statelessness affect WebSocket features?

questions.title: How do you apply dependency inversion and injection in a Node and TypeScript codebase?
questions.quick: I keep business logic dependent on small interfaces that I own, and I pass the real implementations in from the outside. In TypeScript that can be as simple as a constructor taking an interface, with the wiring done in one composition root at start-up. No framework is required. The payoff is that I can test the logic with simple fakes and swap a database or provider without rewriting the core.
questions.revision: Depend on small interfaces you own, pass implementations via constructors, wire them in one composition root. Frameworks are optional; testability is the payoff.
followUps: When is an interface not worth creating?
How would you test PlaceOrder without a database?
What do you gain or lose by using a DI container?

diagrams.title: Dependency direction
diagrams.alt: The controller calls the use case, which depends on interfaces it owns; the MongoDB repository and payment adapter implement those interfaces, so source dependencies point inward toward the business logic.

questions.title: How do you run discovery in a client consulting engagement and turn it into an architecture estimate?
questions.quick: I run discovery as a short, time-boxed phase with clear outputs. I interview stakeholders and users, review existing systems and data, agree goals and constraints, and list assumptions and open questions. Then I sketch a target architecture, identify the riskiest unknowns, and give estimates as ranges tied to assumptions. The client leaves with a shared picture, a prioritised roadmap and the options with costs, not a single magic number.
questions.revision: Time-boxed discovery: stakeholders, current state, goals and constraints, assumptions, risks, target sketch, then range estimates tied to assumptions.
questions.detailed:
Discovery reduces uncertainty **before** a large commitment. In consulting it also builds trust and a shared understanding with the client.

## Activities

1. **Align on goals**: business outcomes, success measures, deadline, budget range.
2. **Stakeholder and user interviews**: sponsors, operations, support, end users.
3. **Current state review**: systems, integrations, data quality, hosting, security and compliance, team skills.
4. **Constraints and assumptions**: write each down and mark who confirms it.
5. **Risk spikes**: short experiments on the riskiest unknowns, such as a legacy API or data migration.
6. **Target architecture sketch**: context and container views plus main decisions and options.
7. **Roadmap and estimate**.

{{diagram:sa-discovery}}

## Outputs

| Output | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Context and container diagrams | Shared picture |
| Assumptions and open questions list | Makes uncertainty visible |
| Risk register | What could change cost or date |
| Options with trade-offs | Lets the client choose |
| Phased roadmap | Early value first |
| Estimate ranges | Honest cost and time |

## Estimating

- Break work into **slices** and estimate each as a **range** (best, likely, worst), or use relative sizing and team throughput.
- Attach each range to the **assumptions** behind it; when an assumption changes, the estimate changes.
- Include non-feature work: environments, security, testing, migration, handover.
- Add an explicit **contingency** proportional to uncertainty, and say so.

## Common mistakes

- Open-ended discovery with no end date or deliverable.
- Giving a single number before assumptions are confirmed.
- Estimating only coding, not testing, deployment and data migration.
- Skipping the people who operate the current system.

Example (hypothetical): discovery shows a legacy customer API is poorly documented; a two-day spike reduces that risk before the estimate is finalised.
followUps: How long should discovery last and how do you decide?
How do you present an estimate range to a client who wants one number?
What do you do if discovery reveals the budget cannot meet the goals?

diagrams.title: Discovery to estimate
diagrams.alt: Discovery moves from goals and stakeholder interviews through current state review, assumptions and risk spikes to a target architecture sketch, then a roadmap and range estimate presented to the client.

questions.title: What would a sensible reference architecture look like for a mid-size MERN product?
questions.quick: I would start simple: a React front end served from a CDN, a Node API structured as a modular monolith, MongoDB with a managed service, and a managed identity provider. Add a queue and a worker for slow or unreliable tasks, a cache only where measured, and centralised logs, metrics and alerts. Split into separate services only when a module needs independent scaling or ownership. Environments and pipelines come early.
questions.revision: CDN-hosted React, modular Node API, managed MongoDB, managed identity, queue plus worker for async work, observability and pipelines from day one; split later if needed.
questions.detailed:
A good reference architecture is **the simplest structure that meets the quality targets**, with clear seams for growth.

## Building blocks

| Layer | Suggested approach | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Front end | React built to static assets, served via CDN | Fast, cheap, scalable |
| API | Node (Express, Fastify or Nest) as a **modular monolith** | One deployable, clear internal modules |
| Data | Managed MongoDB with indexes, backups and schema validation | Less operational work |
| Identity | Managed provider using OIDC; API checks tokens and permissions | Avoid building auth |
| Async work | Queue and worker for emails, imports, reports, webhooks | Keeps requests fast |
| Cache | Add Redis only for measured hot paths | Avoid needless complexity |
| Files | Object storage with signed URLs | Keeps API stateless |
| Observability | Structured logs, metrics, traces, alerts | You cannot fix what you cannot see |
| Delivery | CI pipeline, automated tests, infrastructure as code, preview environments | Safe, repeatable releases |

{{diagram:sa-mern}}

## Design rules

- Modules own their data; others use the module's interface.
- Validate input at the edge; keep a consistent error format.
- Make operations idempotent where retries can occur.
- Separate configuration from code; protect secrets.

## When to split services

Split when a module needs **independent scaling, a separate team, different technology or isolated failure**, not because microservices are fashionable.

## Common mistakes

- Starting with many microservices for a small team.
- Treating MongoDB as schema-free and skipping validation and indexes.
- Keeping sessions or uploads on the API server.
- Skipping observability until the first incident.

Example (hypothetical): an invoicing module that needs heavy report generation moves to a worker consuming a queue, leaving the API unchanged.
followUps: What signals would make you split a module into its own service?
How would you structure the Node modules internally?
What would you put in place before the first production release?

diagrams.title: MERN reference architecture
diagrams.alt: Users reach a CDN-hosted React app, which calls a Node modular monolith API that verifies tokens from an identity provider, stores data in MongoDB, and sends slow work to a queue processed by a worker, with observability across all parts.

questions.title: How do you choose between client-side rendering, server-side rendering and static generation for a React application?
questions.quick: I decide per page from the needs: does it need search visibility, how fast must first content appear, how personalised is it, and how often does it change? Static generation suits content that changes rarely. Server rendering suits public, frequently changing or personalised pages that need search and fast first paint. Client rendering suits logged-in app screens behind authentication. Most products mix all three.
questions.revision: Choose per page: SSG for stable public content, SSR for dynamic public pages needing SEO, CSR for authenticated app screens. Mix them.
questions.detailed:
Rendering strategy is a **per-page decision** driven by search needs, performance, personalisation and operations.

## Comparison

| | CSR (client) | SSR (server) | SSG (static) |
|---|---|---|---|
| HTML built | In the browser | On each request | At build time |
| First content | Slower; needs JS first | Fast | Fastest, from CDN |
| SEO | Weaker unless handled | Good | Good |
| Personalisation | Easy | Possible, needs care with caching | Hard; use client fetching |
| Server cost | Low | Higher, needs compute | Lowest |
| Freshness | Always live via API | Live per request | Stale until rebuild or revalidation |
| Complexity | Lowest | Highest (hydration, server runtime) | Medium (build pipeline) |

{{diagram:sa-render}}

## Decision questions

1. Must search engines index it? Marketing and catalogue pages usually yes; dashboards no.
2. How often does the content change? Rarely suggests SSG; constantly suggests SSR or CSR.
3. Is it personalised per user? That favours CSR or SSR with private caching rules.
4. What is the server budget and team skill with server runtimes?
5. How important is first-load speed on slow devices?

## Hybrid options

- **Incremental regeneration**: static pages refreshed on a schedule or on demand.
- **Streaming and partial rendering**: send the shell first, fill in later.
- Frameworks such as Next.js allow choosing the mode per route.

## Common mistakes

- Using SSR everywhere "for SEO", paying for compute on private pages.
- Caching personalised server-rendered HTML publicly, leaking data.
- Using CSR for a public catalogue and then wondering about search ranking.
- Ignoring hydration cost and bundle size.

Example (hypothetical): a product site uses static pages for marketing, server rendering for product detail with stock, and client rendering for the account area.
followUps: How can personalised server-rendered pages leak data through caching?
What is hydration and why can it hurt performance?
How would you migrate an existing CSR app to a hybrid model?

diagrams.title: Rendering decision
diagrams.alt: Start by asking whether the page must be indexed; if not, use client rendering. If yes, check how often the content changes: rarely changing pages use static generation and frequently changing or personalised pages use server rendering.

questions.title: MongoDB schema design for a MERN product: embed or reference?
questions.quick: I model around how the application reads and writes data. Embed when data is read together, belongs to one parent, and stays bounded in size, such as order lines inside an order. Reference when data is shared, grows without limit, changes independently, or is queried on its own, such as users and orders. I also think about update patterns, the 16 megabyte document limit and consistency needs.
questions.revision: Embed for data read together, owned by one parent and bounded; reference for shared, unbounded or independently queried data. Design for access patterns.
questions.detailed:
MongoDB schema design starts from **access patterns**, not from normalising tables.

## Decision guide

| Question | Favours embedding | Favours referencing |
|---|---|---|
| Read together most of the time? | Yes | No |
| Lifecycle tied to the parent? | Yes | No, independent |
| Size bounded? | Yes, small and predictable | No, can grow without limit |
| Shared by many parents? | No | Yes |
| Updated frequently on its own? | No | Yes |
| Need atomic update with the parent? | Yes (single document is atomic) | Needs a transaction |

## Examples

```js
// Embed: order lines belong to one order and are read with it
{ _id: "o1", customerId: "c9", lines: [{ sku: "A1", qty: 2, pricePence: 500 }] }

// Reference: customer is shared and changes on its own
{ _id: "c9", name: "A. Example", email: "a@example.com" }
```

## Useful patterns

- **Snapshot on write**: copy values that must not change later (the price at purchase) into the order.
- **Subset pattern**: embed only the most recent few items, reference the rest.
- **Bucket pattern**: group time-series or event data into time buckets.
- **Computed fields**: store counts or totals updated on write for read speed.

{{diagram:sa-mongo}}

## Limits to remember

- Documents are capped at 16 MB; unbounded arrays are a smell.
- Large embedded arrays that are updated often cause heavy writes.
- Joins using lookups exist but cost more than single-document reads.
- Add indexes for each query pattern and use schema validation.

## Common mistakes

- Embedding everything, then hitting size and update problems.
- Referencing everything, rebuilding a relational model with slow lookups.
- Forgetting to snapshot prices or addresses, so history changes silently.
- Designing before knowing the queries.

Example (hypothetical): a blog stores comments by reference once threads become large, but embeds the latest three for the list view.
followUps: How do you model a many-to-many relationship in MongoDB?

diagrams.title: Embed or reference
diagrams.alt: If data is read with its parent, owned by it and bounded in size, embed it; otherwise, if it is shared or grows without limit, store it in its own collection and reference it by identifier.
